title: Trumbauer records and the Benson orchestra
summary: Carter recalls hearing Trumbauer first with the Benson orchestra and then on Singin' the Blues.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, one thing struck me in reading Stanley Dance's book which recently came out, which was that a number of musicians who were based in New York described it -- it was much later in their careers when they heard what was described as "Dixieland" music, whatever it is that they mean by Dixieland music, and I was just wondering what kind of music it was that you and the Fletcher Hendersons or the Don Redmonds or the Duke Ellingtons would have been listening to and impressed by. You mentioned Frankie Trumbauer Trombar.

Yes, Frankie Trombar, and I didn't -- I wasn't impressed by too much else of the orchestra with which he was playing. I remember he was playing with the Benson orchestra of Chicago, and the record that I did like of his that I think I even heard before I heard "Singin' The Blues" -- now chronologically, I may be wrong about this, but I think I heard "I'll Never Miss the Sunshine; I'm So Used to the Rain" ...
With the Benson orchestra. Now, of course the other -- "Singin' the Blues" was that Bix Beiderbecke's orchestra?
Yes. Or was it Frankie Trumbauer's orchestra?
I don't know who the nominal leader was.
Yeah, that's right. I don't know either, but I know Bix and Trumbauer were on that thing. Maybe Eddie Lang and some other people, I don't know -- but ...
